How to Tell Whether a Plunging Stock Will Keep Plunging
 
Plus, the yen slides again, and happy retirement Warren Buffett
 

The Fed gets all the headlines, but the U.S. isn’t the only country whose central bank raised interest rates this week. Japan’s hike to a three-decade high was seen as less-convincing, leading to a sharp overnight weakening of the yen. The U.S. recently intervened alongside Japan to strengthen it because of potential knock-on effects. American markets seem to be taking it in stride for now with stocks set for another gain and bond yields stable. Today also marks the end of an era with the news that Warren Buffett will step down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway.

 

​📈 Follow our live markets data and coverage.

9/18/2026, 6:30:16 AM ET
 
 
 

Missing the bounce

 

One of the oldest pieces of Wall Street wisdom is not to try catching a falling knife—a stock that’s plunging. They can keep going longer and more violently than investors expect.

 

But what if you already own it? Many investors, especially hedge fund traders, use stop-loss orders to limit the damage to their portfolios. 

 

The downside to that cut-and-run approach is that in some cases they’ll lock in an initial panic loss. Then the former owners miss out on a big rebound. If the trend of falling stocks having downward momentum were consistent then making outright bets against them would be a sure-fire trading strategy, and it isn’t.

 

Adam Parker and his team at Trivariate Research looked at thousands of sharp drawdowns over a quarter century to glean clues about when quickly dropping stocks tend to keep falling. To keep the results relevant, they excluded pharma and biotech where drug approval headlines can have extreme results. They also avoided the most turbulent periods such as the Covid-19 panic and financial crisis.

 

One interesting finding is that the stocks that fell most sharply or quickly relative to their industry peers tended to underperform by nearly 9% in the coming year. Those that just fell relative to the overall stock market often recover fully.

 

Late 2023 offers an example. The effectiveness of GLP-1 weight loss drugs sparked a panic that October, hitting purveyors of caloric food and beverages such as Coca-Cola, Pepsico, Yum Brands and Mondelez. 

 

They all fell by between 6% and 15% in just a few days, but each one recovered by year-end. Potato chip maker Utz’s shares bounced by 42% from their October low.

 

A more recent example is this February’s “SaaSpocalypse” when AI coding advances sent software stocks such as ServiceNow, Salesforce and DocuSign plunging. It was a great buying opportunity in most cases.

 

The reason for a selloff matters too, according to Trivariate. Sharp downturns tend to stick when they’re related to disappointing earnings as opposed to something else. Only 36% of stock plunges relative to their industry were earnings related.

 

And not every company is as prone to becoming a falling knife. Value stocks—defined by Trivariate as the cheapest fifth of stocks by forward price/earnings—enjoy some degree of buoyancy after a big drop.

 

As hard as it is to pick stocks, deciding whether to sell them, and when, is even tougher. Behavioral biases can tug investors in the direction of either panicking and holding on following a plunge. We dread more losses but mentally anchor a stock’s value to an old price that may have become meaningless.

 

Having an evidence-based framework could make the decision easier and more rewarding.

↗️ Sandoz Group: The Swiss maker of generic drugs said it received approval from Canada’s drug regulator for its generic version of Novo Nordisk’s Ozempic, advancing its efforts to build a portfolio of GLP-1 medicines. Shares rose 2% in Switzerland.

 

↘️ Nike: Shares of the sports-apparel retailer retreated premarket ahead of its deletion from the S&P 100 index of large-cap companies on Sept. 21.

 

↗️ Coinbase Global, Robinhood Markets, Strategy: Shares of companies tied to cryptocurrencies jumped premarket as bitcoin’s price advanced beyond $78,000, up more than 2% from its 4 p.m. ET level Thursday.

 

↗️ Corning, Intel, Alphabet: Shares of companies tied to AI jumped premarket, as investors returned to a strategy that has worked time and again this year.
